title: Chemistry 11 · Legacy Concept Spine Misconception Map
coveragePolicy: reviewed-subset; newly authored or substantially revised selected-response items should include complete mapping

legacy-01.prompt: Atomic number is determined by the number of
legacy-01.correctRationale: Element identity is defined by proton number.

distractors.rationale: Neutron count changes isotope mass, but proton count defines the element.
Electron-shell arrangement can affect chemical behavior, but it does not define atomic number.
Isotopes are variants of one element; the number of isotopes is not an atom's atomic number.

legacy-02.prompt: Isotopes of an element differ in their number of
legacy-02.correctRationale: Isotopes share proton number but differ in neutron number.

distractors.rationale: Changing proton number changes the element itself rather than producing an isotope of the same element.
Valence rules describe electron behavior; they are not a particle count that distinguishes isotopes.
Isotopes of one element share the same element symbol; the distinguishing particle count is neutrons.

legacy-03.prompt: A line spectrum supports the idea that electron energies are
legacy-03.correctRationale: Discrete spectral lines are evidence for quantized energy differences.

distractors.rationale: A continuous-energy model would not naturally produce discrete spectral lines.
Atomic emission and absorption spectra arise from electronic energy changes in atoms.
Electrons can occupy different allowed energy states; the evidence does not imply their energy is always zero.

legacy-04.prompt: Across a period, recurring chemical patterns are strongly related to
legacy-04.correctRationale: Valence-electron patterns help explain periodic behavior.

distractors.rationale: Atomic mass does not by itself explain the repeating chemical patterns across a period.
Neutrons do not have a chemical 'color' that governs periodic behavior.
Laboratory glassware does not determine intrinsic periodic trends.

legacy-05.prompt: An ionic compound is electrically neutral when

distractors.rationale: Ionic compounds contain charged ions; neutrality applies to the total formula unit, not each ion.
Ions still contain electrons; charge reflects an imbalance between protons and electrons.
Charge balance is a property of the compound's formula and does not require dissolution.

legacy-06.prompt: A covalent bond is modeled primarily as
legacy-06.correctRationale: Covalent bonding involves shared electron density.

distractors.rationale: Ordinary covalent bonding involves valence electrons, not transfer of neutrons between nuclei.
Nuclear fission changes nuclei and is not the mechanism of a covalent bond.
Gravitational attraction is negligible at molecular scale compared with electromagnetic interactions.

legacy-07.correctRationale: Bond dipoles can reinforce or cancel depending on geometry.

distractors.rationale: Molecular mass alone cannot determine polarity; bond dipoles and geometry control the net dipole.
Color is not a defining criterion for molecular polarity.
A substance's state of matter does not by itself determine whether an individual molecule is polar.

legacy-08.prompt: Metals conduct electricity well in part because
legacy-08.correctRationale: Mobile electrons are part of the metallic-bonding model.

distractors.optionText: all metal atoms are ions in solution
distractors.rationale: Electrical conduction in a metal does not require the metal atoms to be dissolved as ions.
Metal atoms contain nuclei; conduction is explained by mobile electrons in the metallic structure.
Most metals are solid under ordinary conditions, yet many still conduct well.

legacy-09.prompt: Hydrogen bonding is especially important when H is bonded to
legacy-09.correctRationale: Strongly polar N–H, O–H, and F–H bonds enable hydrogen bonding.

distractors.rationale: Hydrogen bonding requires a strongly polarized H bonded to highly electronegative atoms such as N, O, or F, not simply any metal.
Noble gases generally do not form the strongly polar H–X bonds required for conventional hydrogen bonding.
A C–H bond is usually not polar enough to produce the strong hydrogen bonding described here.

legacy-10.prompt: At constant temperature, decreasing gas volume generally causes pressure to
legacy-10.correctRationale: Less volume increases collision frequency with container walls.

distractors.rationale: At constant temperature, reducing volume increases wall-collision frequency, so pressure rises rather than falls.
Compression does not make gas pressure exactly zero.
Gas pressure is directly related to particle collisions with container walls in the kinetic model.
Molarity uses moles of solute divided by liters of total solution, not grams of solvent per mole.
Liters per atom is not the concentration definition of molarity.
Moles per gram is a mass-normalized ratio, not molarity, which is volume-normalized.

legacy-12.prompt: Chromatography separates mixture components because they
legacy-12.correctRationale: Different relative attractions produce different migration.

distractors.rationale: If components interacted identically with both phases, they would migrate similarly and separation would be poor.
Chromatography is a physical/chemical partitioning method, not a nuclear process.
Chromatographic migration does not require every component to lose all electrons.

legacy-13.prompt: Balancing a chemical equation enforces conservation of
legacy-13.correctRationale: Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed in ordinary reactions.

distractors.rationale: Coefficients are adjusted to represent conservation; the conserved entities are atoms of each element.
Balancing an equation does not require temperature to remain constant.
Phase labels describe physical state; they are not the conserved count enforced by balancing.

legacy-14.correctRationale: The Avogadro constant relates moles to number of entities.

distractors.rationale: 9.81 is associated with gravitational acceleration near Earth, not the number of entities in a mole.
A mole is not defined as exactly 100 entities.
1.60×10^-19 is associated with elementary charge magnitude in coulombs, not Avogadro's constant.

legacy-15.prompt: The limiting reactant is the reactant that
legacy-15.correctRationale: It limits the maximum amount of product.

distractors.rationale: The limiting reactant depends on available amounts relative to stoichiometric ratios, not simply on largest molar mass.
A limiting reactant can be solid, liquid, gas, or dissolved; phase does not define the role.
Limiting-reactant analysis depends on measured or specified amounts; the limiting reactant is not defined as unmeasured.
Atomic number and mass number describe nuclei and are unrelated to percent yield.
Temperature-to-pressure comparison is not the definition of percent yield.
Electron and neutron counts do not define reaction yield.

legacy-17.correctRationale: Oxidation tracks electron loss/increased oxidation state.

distractors.rationale: Oxidation in ordinary chemistry concerns electron transfer or oxidation state, not gain of neutrons.
Oxidation is not defined by a universal decrease in energy.

distractors.optionText: formation of water in every reaction
distractors.rationale: Many oxidation reactions do not form water; water production is not the defining criterion.

legacy-18.prompt: Reaction rate is often determined from

distractors.rationale: Atomic number divided by mass is not a reaction-rate measurement.
Color can be a proxy only when related to concentration or extent by a calibrated measurement; color alone is insufficient.
Counting equations written measures neither chemical change nor elapsed time.

legacy-19.correctRationale: Catalysts alter pathway/activation energy, not net thermodynamics.

distractors.optionText: raising the equilibrium constant in every case
distractors.rationale: A catalyst speeds forward and reverse pathways without changing the equilibrium constant at a fixed temperature.
A catalyst participates in a mechanism but is regenerated rather than consumed as a net stoichiometric reactant.
Catalysis changes pathway and rate; it does not create atoms.

legacy-20.prompt: Increasing temperature often speeds a reaction because
legacy-20.correctRationale: Higher temperature changes collision energy distribution.

distractors.rationale: Higher temperature increases average kinetic energy rather than stopping particle motion.
Heating changes the energy distribution; it does not make the activation energy itself zero.
Temperature can shift an equilibrium, but it does not mean equilibrium is always destroyed.

legacy-21.prompt: In calorimetry, q=mcΔT relates heat to
legacy-21.correctRationale: This relation estimates heat transfer from measurable quantities.

distractors.rationale: The equation q=mcΔT contains no pressure term; it relates heat to mass, specific heat, and temperature change.
Moles can enter other thermochemical relations, but q=mcΔT is not defined by moles alone.
Atomic number does not appear in the calorimetry relation.

legacy-22.prompt: Hess's law works because enthalpy is
legacy-22.correctRationale: State functions depend on initial/final states, not path.

distractors.rationale: A catalyst is a substance or pathway feature; enthalpy is a thermodynamic state function.
An isotope is a nuclear variant of an element, not a thermodynamic property.
Enthalpy is an energy quantity, not a unit of pressure.

legacy-23.correctRationale: Entropy tracks energy/matter dispersal and multiplicity.

distractors.rationale: Greater entropy is not defined as absence of motion; microscopic motion and accessible arrangements are central to statistical descriptions.
Electron charge is an electrical property, not the thermodynamic meaning of entropy.
Molar mass alone does not define entropy.

legacy-24.correctRationale: Macroscopic constancy can coexist with ongoing microscopic change.

distractors.rationale: Dynamic equilibrium still has ongoing molecular motion and forward/reverse events.
Reactants and products can both remain present at nonzero concentrations at equilibrium.
Dynamic equilibrium requires both forward and reverse processes, not only the forward direction.

legacy-25.correctRationale: It provides a qualitative response model.

distractors.optionText: the exact mechanism of every reaction
distractors.rationale: Le Châtelier reasoning predicts directional response to disturbance; it does not reveal an exact reaction mechanism.
Nuclear half-life is governed by radioactive decay, not Le Châtelier's principle.
Atomic number is a nuclear identity property and is not predicted by equilibrium-shift reasoning.

legacy-26.prompt: A buffer resists pH change because it contains
legacy-26.correctRationale: A conjugate pair can moderate added H+ or OH−.

distractors.rationale: Pure water has limited capacity to consume added acid or base and is not a conjugate buffer system.
Buffer action generally depends on acid/base species and their conjugates, often present as ions.
Radioactive isotopes are unrelated to the acid–base mechanism by which buffers resist pH change.

legacy-27.prompt: A decrease of one pH unit corresponds to about

distractors.rationale: A one-unit pH change refers to a tenfold hydrogen-ion concentration change, not a twofold mass change.
Neutron number is a nuclear property and does not define pH.
Because pH is logarithmic, a one-unit decrease does imply a concentration change; it is not 'no change.'

legacy-28.correctRationale: Separated redox half-reactions can drive electron flow.

distractors.rationale: A galvanic cell does not convert electrical energy into gravity; it produces electrical energy from a spontaneous redox process.

distractors.optionText: nuclear energy into mass loss only
distractors.rationale: Galvanic cells operate through chemical redox reactions rather than nuclear mass conversion.
Sound-to-atom conversion is not the operating principle of an electrochemical cell.

legacy-29.prompt: Radioactive decay differs from an ordinary chemical reaction because it changes

distractors.rationale: Ordinary chemical reactions can change intermolecular interactions; radioactive decay is distinguished by a change in the nucleus.
Solution volume can change in ordinary physical or chemical processes and does not define radioactive decay.
Molecular orientation changes do not constitute radioactive nuclear transformation.

legacy-30.prompt: A sustainable materials decision should consider
legacy-30.correctRationale: Engineering decisions require multiple criteria and tradeoffs.

distractors.rationale: Purchase price alone ignores lifecycle impacts, performance, safety, and uncertainty.
Color can be a design consideration but cannot by itself establish sustainability or engineering suitability.
Molar mass alone does not capture performance, lifecycle, safety, cost, or uncertainty tradeoffs.
